claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 base editor version 3 (BE3) consists of an engineered fusion of Cas9 and a cytidine deaminase that converts cytosine to uracil, thereby effecting a C-to-T substitution at a target site defined by the guide RNA.
source: To introduce genetic perturbations across the yeast genome in a targeted fashion, we used the CRISPR base editor version 3 (BE3) (Komor et al., 2016). This system consists of an engineered fusion of Cas9 and a cytidine deaminase that does not introduce DNA double-strand breaks but instead converts cytosine to uracil, thereby effecting a C-to-T substitution at a target site defined by the guide RNA (gRNA) (Komor et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by citation to Komor et al., 2016, which describes the BE3 system.

claim: In yeast, 95% of base edits are C-to-T transitions.
source: We found that the target window and mutagenesis pattern are very similar to those described in human cells: 95% of edits are C-to-T transitions, and 89% of these occurred in a five-nucleotide window 13–17 base pairs upstream of the PAM sequence (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Komor et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from amplicon sequencing of eight individual gRNAs after base editor expression, as shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 89% of C-to-T edits in yeast occurred in a five-nucleotide window 13–17 base pairs upstream of the PAM sequence.
source: We found that the target window and mutagenesis pattern are very similar to those described in human cells: 95% of edits are C-to-T transitions, and 89% of these occurred in a five-nucleotide window 13–17 base pairs upstream of the PAM sequence (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Komor et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from amplicon sequencing and comparison to human cell data from Komor et al., 2016.

claim: Base editing efficiency in yeast ranged from 4% to 64% across eight gRNAs when considering only cases where all Cs in the window are edited.
source: Editing efficiency was variable across the eight gRNAs and ranged from 4% to 64% if considering only cases where all Cs in the window are edited; percentages are higher if incomplete edits are considered, too (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from amplicon sequencing shown in Figure 1B.

claim: By 24 hours after induction of base editor expression, a majority of cells in which GFP was targeted had lost the GFP signal.
source: Depending on the gRNA, cells lost the GFP signal at different rates; however, for both gRNAs, a majority of cells had lost the GFP signal after 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring GFP fluorescence over time, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the canavanine screen, there was a strong enrichment of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce premature stop codons (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1737, df=1).
source: We exposed base-edited yeast cultures to canavanine for 24 and 48 hr and observed a strong enrichment of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce premature stop codons (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1737, df=1, chi-squared test), as well as a depletion of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce synonymous mutations in CAN1 (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1637, df=1, chi-squared test) (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the canavanine resistance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: In the canavanine screen, there was a depletion of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce synonymous mutations in CAN1 (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1637, df=1).
source: We exposed base-edited yeast cultures to canavanine for 24 and 48 hr and observed a strong enrichment of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce premature stop codons (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1737, df=1, chi-squared test), as well as a depletion of reads from gRNAs predicted to introduce synonymous mutations in CAN1 (p<2.2e-16, χ2=1637, df=1, chi-squared test) (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the canavanine resistance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: Seven of the eleven missense mutations with a strong effect in CAN1 have a PROVEAN score <–5, indicating high conservation (p=0.007, OR=0.15).
source: Most of these missense mutations with a strong effect are at highly conserved amino acid residues, as reflected by their more negative PROVEAN scores (Choi et al., 2012); seven of the eleven amino acid substitutions have a PROVEAN score <–5, indicating high conservation (p=0.007, OR=0.15, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the canavanine screen combined with PROVEAN conservation scores from Choi et al., 2012.

claim: In the fitness screen, 59% of gRNAs introducing stop codons into essential genes displayed log2 fold change <–0.5 and FDR for depletion <0.05.
source: As expected, cells transformed with control gRNAs remained in the culture at stable levels, whereas cells transformed with gRNAs introducing stop codons into essential genes tended to drop out over time (59% displayed log2 fold change <–0.5 and false-discovery rate (FDR) for depletion <0.05) (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the fitness screen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A lasso regression model with over 8000 sequence features per gRNA could explain 37% of the observed variance in gRNA depletion in the screen of essential genes (Pearson's R2=0.37, p<2.2e-16).
source: To address this, we built a lasso regression model with over 8000 sequence features per gRNA and found that it could explain 37% of the observed variance in gRNA depletion in the screen of essential genes (Pearson's R2=0.37, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of experimental data from the fitness screen.

claim: The base preceding the target C has a strong effect on editing efficiency, with a T or another C producing much higher editing rates than a G.
source: In particular, the base preceding the target C has a strong effect—a T or another C produces much higher editing rates than a G. These findings in yeast are in line with recent reports in human cell lines and can help guide the design of future gRNA libraries (Arbab et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the lasso regression model and is consistent with findings in human cell lines from Arbab et al., 2020 and Song et al., 2020.

claim: The base editor screen identified 1020 gRNAs with a significant effect on the abundance of at least one of the eleven proteins (FDR<0.05).
source: We identified 1020 gRNAs with a significant effect on the abundance of at least one of the eleven proteins (FDR<0.05) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: Effects of gRNAs in replicate experiments showed significant correlation (Pearson's R2=0.37, p<2.2e-16).
source: Effects of gRNAs in replicate experiments showed significant correlation (Pearson's R2=0.37, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of replicate experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For 78 gRNA pairs predicted to introduce the same mutation, where at least one gRNA had a significant effect, their effects were well correlated (Pearson's R2=0.43, p<2.2e-16).
source: For 78 of these gRNA pairs, at least one gRNA had a significant effect (FDR<0.05) on at least one of the eleven proteins; their effects were well correlated (Pearson's R2=0.43, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of gRNA pairs targeting the same mutation, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For 20 gRNA pairs in which both gRNAs had a significant effect, the correlation was even higher (Pearson's R2=0.81, p=8.8e-13).
source: For the 20 gRNA pairs in which both gRNAs had a significant effect, the correlation was even higher (Pearson's R2=0.81, p=8.8e-13) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of gRNA pairs where both had significant effects, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The effects of genetic perturbations on protein abundances correlate well with the effects on mRNA abundances measured in an earlier study (Kemmeren et al., 2014) when considering only effects that are significant in both studies (Pearson's R2=0.62, p<5.3e-15).
source: The effects of genetic perturbations on protein abundances correlate well with the effects on mRNA abundances measured in an earlier study (Kemmeren et al., 2014) when considering only effects that are significant in both studies (Pearson's R2=0.62, p<5.3e-15) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of protein abundance data from this study with mRNA abundance data from Kemmeren et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic perturbation of 710 genes had a significant effect on the abundance of at least one of the eleven proteins (FDR<0.05).
source: Genetic perturbation of 710 genes had a significant effect on the abundance of at least one of the eleven proteins (FDR<0.05) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen after combining gRNA effects into gene-level effects.

claim: On average, the abundance of a protein was significantly affected by 156 gene perturbations.
source: On average, the abundance of a protein was significantly affected by 156 gene perturbations (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Of the gene-protein relationships, an average of 53 (34%) are specific (affecting only one or two of the eleven target proteins) whereas 103 (66%) are nonspecific (affecting three or more of the eleven proteins).
source: Of these gene-protein relationships, an average of 53 (34%) are specific (defined here as gene perturbations that affect only one or two of the eleven target proteins) whereas 103 (66%) are nonspecific (the gene perturbation affects three or more of the eleven proteins).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: On average, protein abundance decreases more frequently than it increases in response to the gene perturbations tested (106 vs 50, p=8.6e-6).
source: Furthermore, we found that, on average, protein abundance decreases more frequently than it increases in response to the gene perturbations tested (106 vs 50, p=8.6e-6, binomial test) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: Abundance of proteins involved in core cellular functions mostly decreases (p=2.9e-12), whereas abundance of stress-related proteins is just as likely to increase as it is to decrease (p=0.8).
source: However, this trend is strongly dependent on the functional role of the protein. Abundance of proteins involved in core cellular functions mostly decreases, whereas abundance of stress-related proteins is just as likely to increase as it is to decrease (p=2.9e-12 and p=0.8, respectively, binomial test) (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: Perturbations in essential genes on average decrease protein abundance in 80% of cases, whereas perturbations in nonessential genes do so in only 49% of cases.
source: The predominance of decreases in protein abundance in response to gene perturbations is driven by perturbations in essential genes, which on average decrease protein abundance in 80% of cases, whereas perturbations in nonessential genes do so in only 49% of cases (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Perturbations in essential genes are generally more likely to significantly alter protein abundance than are perturbations in nonessential genes (p<2.2e-16, χ2=384, df=1).
source: Furthermore, perturbations in essential genes are generally more likely to significantly alter protein abundance than are perturbations in nonessential genes (p<2.2e-16, χ2=384, df=1, chi-squared test) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: For nonessential genes, premature stop codons are more likely to alter protein abundance than are missense mutations (p=1.2e-9, χ2=37, df=1).
source: For nonessential genes, premature stop codons are more likely to alter protein abundance than are missense mutations (p=1.2e-9, χ2=37, df=1, chi-squared test) (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: The average effect size of changes caused by stop codons is larger than that caused by missense mutations (p=0.0028, t=–3.0, df=496).
source: and the average effect size of changes caused by stop codons is larger (p=0.0028, t=–3.0, df=496, two-sided t-test) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen with statistical analysis.

claim: Mutations towards the end of a gene tend to have fewer and smaller effects.
source: We also find that mutations towards the end of a gene tend to have fewer and smaller effects, in line with previous observations (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Sadhu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and is consistent with previous observations from Sadhu et al., 2018.

claim: Perturbation of Gcr1, a key transcription factor for glycolytic genes, leads to reduced Eno2 abundance, consistent with its role as a transcriptional activator.
source: Perturbation of Gcr1, a key transcription factor for glycolytic genes, leads to reduced Eno2 abundance, consistent with its role as a transcriptional activator (Baker, 1986; Holland et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and is consistent with known roles from Baker, 1986 and Holland et al., 1987.

claim: Histone Htb2 abundance is strongly reduced upon perturbation of known regulators of histone gene transcription (Hir3, Spt10, Spt21).
source: Similarly, histone Htb2 abundance is strongly reduced upon perturbation of known regulators of histone gene transcription (Hir3, Spt10, Spt21) (Kurat et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and is consistent with known roles from Kurat et al., 2014.

claim: Ribosomal protein Rpl9A abundance is strongly reduced upon perturbation of other ribosomal genes, as well as of genes involved in TOR signaling (Tor2, Asa1, Kog1, Rtc1, Sch9).
source: Ribosomal protein Rpl9A abundance is also strongly reduced upon perturbation of other ribosomal genes, as well as of genes involved in TOR signaling (Tor2, Asa1, Kog1, Rtc1, Sch9), including the TOR-regulated activators of ribosomal gene transcription, Fhl1 and Ifh1, which are known to act together with the broad transcription factor Rap1 to induce expression of ribosomal genes (Rudra et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and is consistent with known roles from Rudra et al., 2005.

claim: The abundance of the stress-responsive flavohemoglobin/oxidoreductase Yhb1 is reduced by perturbation of one of its prime transcriptional activators, heme activator protein Hap1, as well as perturbations of a heme transporter and six genes involved in heme biosynthesis.
source: For example, the abundance of the stress-responsive flavohemoglobin/oxidoreductase Yhb1 is reduced by perturbation of one of its prime transcriptional activators, heme activator protein Hap1, as well as perturbations of a heme transporter and six genes involved in heme biosynthesis (Cassanova et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and is consistent with known roles from Cassanova et al., 2005.

claim: Yhb1 is a heme protein.
source: This is in accordance with Yhb1 being a heme protein itself (Zhu and Riggs, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu and Riggs, 1992.

claim: Perturbation of each of the three subunits of the Ssy1-Ptr3-Ssy5 (SPS) amino acid sensor, as well as of one of its two downstream effectors, the transcription factor Stp1, results in reduced Yhb1 abundance.
source: A novel regulator of Yhb1 identified in our screen is the three-subunit Ssy1-Ptr3-Ssy5 (SPS) amino acid sensor. We find that perturbation of each of the three subunits, as well as of one of its two downstream effectors, the transcription factor Stp1, results in reduced Yhb1 abundance (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LC-MS proteomics analysis of the SSY5 G638Q mutant confirmed reduced Yhb1 abundance.
source: We independently confirmed the new regulatory relationship between Yhb1 and SPS by liquid-chromatography-coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) proteomics analysis of one of the SPS mutants identified in our screen, SSY5 G638Q (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent validation using LC-MS proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SPS perturbation leads to reduced abundance of mitochondrial proteins, including components of the mitochondrial ribosome, oxidative phosphorylation, and ATP metabolism (FDR=4.5e-4).
source: Furthermore, gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of differentially expressed proteins in this mutant revealed that SPS perturbation leads not only to reduced Yhb1 abundance but also to reduced abundance of other mitochondrial proteins, including components of the mitochondrial ribosome, oxidative phosphorylation, and ATP metabolism (FDR=4.5e-4, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of LC-MS proteomics data from the SSY5 G638Q mutant shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Amino acid metabolic processes are broadly induced in the SSY5 G638Q mutant (FDR=6.6e-9).
source: In contrast, amino acid metabolic processes are broadly induced in the mutant (FDR=6.6e-9, Figure 4C), suggesting that SPS signaling not just activates expression of amino acid transporters but also represses amino acid biosynthesis (Forsberg et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of LC-MS proteomics data from the SSY5 G638Q mutant shown in Figure 4C, and is consistent with findings from Forsberg et al., 2001.

claim: The presence of extracellular amino acids has been found to induce Yhb1 expression in the distantly related yeast Candida albicans.
source: Recently, the presence of extracellular amino acids has been found to induce Yhb1 expression in the distantly related yeast Candida albicans (Danhof et al., 2016; Williams and Lorenz, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Danhof et al., 2016 and Williams and Lorenz, 2020.

claim: SPS senses the presence of external amino acids and activates the transcription factor Stp1, which in turn induces Yhb1 expression, resulting in increased nitrosative and oxidative stress resistance.
source: We propose that SPS senses the presence of external amino acids and activates the transcription factor Stp1, which in turn induces Yhb1 expression, resulting in increased nitrosative and oxidative stress resistance (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data from the protein abundance screen and LC-MS proteomics.

claim: Perturbation of two subunits of the Cdk8 kinase module of mediator, Ssn3 and Srb8, causes particularly large effects on three proteins (Htb2, Tdh1, and Tdh2).
source: We find particularly large effects on three proteins (Htb2, Tdh1, and Tdh2) upon perturbation of two subunits of the Cdk8 kinase module of mediator, Ssn3 and Srb8 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Perturbations of the two subunits forming the hook structure on mediator, Nut2 and Rox3, cause large effects on Htb2, Tdh1, and Tdh2.
source: Moreover, we see large effects on the same proteins for perturbations of the two subunits forming the hook structure on mediator, Nut2 and Rox3, which supports recent reports that this domain is critical for the interaction between the core mediator complex and the Cdk8 kinase module (Figure 4D; Tsai et al., 2014; Tsai et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 4D and is consistent with findings from Tsai et al., 2014 and Tsai et al., 2013.

claim: The observation that perturbations of the Cdk8 module increase protein abundance is in accordance with the suggested repressor role of this transiently associating regulatory module of mediator.
source: The observation that perturbations of the Cdk8 module increase protein abundance is in accordance with the suggested repressor role of this transiently associating regulatory module of mediator (Elmlund et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and is consistent with the suggested role from Elmlund et al., 2006.

claim: Ssa1 and Yhb1 are significantly induced upon perturbation of a number of genes involved in proteasomal degradation.
source: We also find that classical post-transcriptional regulators contribute strongly to protein abundance. For example, Ssa1 and Yhb1 are significantly induced upon perturbation of a number of genes involved in proteasomal degradation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Perturbations in 29 genes significantly alter the abundance of eight or more proteins.
source: For instance, perturbations in 29 genes significantly alter the abundance of eight or more proteins (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Of the 29 genes with broad effects on protein abundance, 21 (72%) have roles in protein translation—more specifically, in ribosome biogenesis and tRNA metabolism (FDR<8.0e-4).
source: Of these 29 genes, 21 (72%) have roles in protein translation—more specifically, in ribosome biogenesis and tRNA metabolism (FDR<8.0e-4, Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Perturbations that affect the abundance of only one or two of the eleven proteins mostly occur in genes with roles in transcription (e.g., GO:0006351, FDR<1.3e-5).
source: In contrast, perturbations that affect the abundance of only one or two of the eleven proteins mostly occur in genes with roles in transcription (e.g., GO:0006351, FDR<1.3e-5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen and GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes with post-transcriptional functions are more likely to appear as hubs in protein regulatory networks, whereas genes with transcriptional functions are likely to show fewer connections.
source: Thus, genes with post-transcriptional functions are more likely to appear as hubs in protein regulatory networks, whereas genes with transcriptional functions are likely to show fewer connections.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that perturbations of translational machinery alter protein abundance broadly, while perturbations of transcriptional machinery tune individual proteins.

claim: POP1 is an essential gene involved in ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA) maturation.
source: One of the broadest regulators is POP1, an essential gene involved in ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA) maturation (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about POP1 function.

claim: LC-MS proteomics confirmed that missense mutation H642Y in POP1 leads to reduced abundance of most of the eleven proteins under study.
source: We used LC-MS proteomics to independently confirm that missense mutation H642Y in POP1 leads to reduced abundance of most of the eleven proteins under study (Figure 5D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent validation using LC-MS proteomics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Perturbation of POP1 reduces the abundance of many proteins in the nucleolus (FDR=0.013).
source: Furthermore, the proteomics data revealed that perturbation of POP1 reduces the abundance of many proteins in the nucleolus (FDR=0.013, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the role of POP1 in rRNA and tRNA processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of LC-MS proteomics data from the POP1 H642Y mutant shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Perturbation of POP1 induces a large number of proteins involved in amino acid biosynthesis (FDR=1.4e-13).
source: We also see the induction of a large number of proteins involved in amino acid biosynthesis (FDR=1.4e-13, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of LC-MS proteomics data from the POP1 H642Y mutant shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All but three of the 29 gene perturbations with broad effects on protein abundance generally lowered protein abundance.
source: All but three of the 29 gene perturbations with broad effects on protein abundance generally lowered protein abundance (Figure 5B and C, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: One of the three genes whose perturbation increased protein abundance is the PP2A-like phosphatase SIT4.
source: One of the three genes whose perturbation increased protein abundance is the PP2A-like phosphatase SIT4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: Perturbation of SAP155, a gene strictly required for the function of SIT4, has very similar effects on protein abundance to perturbation of SIT4.
source: Perturbation of SAP155, a gene strictly required for the function of SIT4, has very similar effects on protein abundance (Figure 5B, right panel) (Luke et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 5B and is consistent with the known relationship from Luke et al., 1996.

claim: LC-MS proteomics of a SIT4 loss-of-function mutant (Q184*) revealed the induction of a large number of proteins involved in cellular respiration, carbohydrate metabolism, and oxidative stress (FDR <0.01).
source: LC-MS proteomics of a SIT4 loss-of-function mutant (Q184*) revealed the induction of a large number of proteins involved in cellular respiration, carbohydrate metabolism, and oxidative stress (FDR <0.01, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of LC-MS proteomics data from the SIT4 Q184* mutant shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gene perturbations with broader effects on protein abundance were more likely to impair cellular fitness (Pearson's R2=0.18, p<2.2e-16).
source: We observed that gene perturbations with broader effects on protein abundance were more likely to impair cellular fitness (Pearson's R2=0.18, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of protein abundance screen data with fitness screen data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Gene perturbations with broader effects on protein abundance were more likely to be in essential genes.
source: Consistent with this finding, these perturbations were also more likely to be in essential genes (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Essential genes are often involved in maintaining general cellular physiology, so their perturbation is expected to have more widespread effects on protein abundance than perturbation of nonessential genes.
source: Because essential genes are often involved in maintaining general cellular physiology, their perturbation is expected to have more widespread effects on protein abundance than perturbation of nonessential genes that may function in niche processes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge about essential genes.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the connectivity of a gene product and the change in cellular growth rate upon gene deletion.
source: This is also in line with earlier observations that essential genes are more interconnected in protein-protein interaction networks (network hubs), and that there is a negative correlation between the connectivity of a gene product and the change in cellular growth rate upon gene deletion (Batada et al., 2006; Jeong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Batada et al., 2006 and Jeong et al., 2001.

claim: The base editor screen identified candidate causal genes for 24 eQTL and pQTL hotspots.
source: Thus, the base editor screen identified candidate causal genes for 24 eQTL and pQTL hotspots (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of protein abundance screen data with previously identified eQTL and pQTL hotspots.

claim: POP1 overlaps a protein regulatory hotspot on chromosome 14 and harbors several coding variants in divergent yeast strains.
source: One such causal gene candidate is POP1, which overlaps a protein regulatory hotspot on chromosome 14 (Albert et al., 2014) and harbors several coding variants in divergent yeast strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with pQTL data from Albert et al., 2014 and genetic variant data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tdh3 is thought to be the main GAPDH enzyme in glycolysis and is one of the most highly expressed proteins.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Tdh3 is thought to be the main GAPDH enzyme in glycolysis and is one of the most highly expressed proteins (Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Newman et al., 2006.

claim: A functional copy of either TDH2 or TDH3 is required for cell viability.
source: None of the three GAPDH genes are essential for cell viability, but a functional copy of either TDH2 or TDH3 is required; in contrast, cells with a TDH1 deletion, either alone or in combination with a TDH2 or a TDH3 deletion, are viable (McAlister and Holland, 1985b; McAlister and Holland, 1985a; Randez-Gil et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McAlister and Holland, 1985b; McAlister and Holland, 1985a; and Randez-Gil et al., 2019.

claim: The three GAPDH isoenzymes were shown to selectively change abundance in response to available carbon sources and other environmental perturbations.
source: The three isoenzymes were shown to selectively change abundance in response to available carbon sources and other environmental perturbations (Casanovas et al., 2015; Costenoble et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2015; Valadi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casanovas et al., 2015; Costenoble et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2015; and Valadi et al., 2004.

claim: Perturbation of genes encoding two members of the Mediator Cdk8 module, Ssn3 and Srb8, affect abundance of Tdh1 and Tdh2 but not Tdh3.
source: For example, perturbation of genes encoding two members of the Mediator Cdk8 module, Ssn3 and Srb8, affect abundance of Tdh1 and Tdh2 but not Tdh3 (Figures 6A and 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figures 6A and 4D.

claim: Ssn3 and Srb8 have been implicated in carbon catabolite repression.
source: Ssn3 and Srb8 have been implicated in carbon catabolite repression, a mechanism to repress genes involved in the use of alternate carbon sources when a preferred carbon source such as glucose is available (Kayikci and Nielsen, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kayikci and Nielsen, 2015.

claim: Tdh3 is thought to be the main enzyme responsible for glycolytic flux under high-glucose conditions.
source: Because Tdh3 is thought to be the main enzyme responsible for glycolytic flux under high-glucose conditions, it is plausible that the alternative enzymes Tdh1 and Tdh2 are under carbon catabolite repression and play a role when glucose is unavailable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge about Tdh3 function and experimental observations.

claim: Tdh1 is strongly induced in the absence of glucose.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with strong induction of Tdh1 in the absence of glucose (Casanovas et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casanovas et al., 2015 and Murphy et al., 2015.

claim: Perturbations of activating components of the Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway (Gpr1, Ras2, Cyr1, Cdc25) increase abundance of Tdh1 but decrease abundance of Tdh2 (and, to a lesser extent, Tdh3).
source: Perturbations of activating components of this pathway (Gpr1, Ras2, Cyr1, Cdc25) increase abundance of Tdh1 but decrease abundance of Tdh2 (and, to a lesser extent, Tdh3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: Perturbation of the farnesyl pyrophosphate synthetase Erg20 increases abundance of Tdh1 but decreases abundance of Tdh2.
source: Perturbation of the farnesyl pyrophosphate synthetase Erg20 had the same effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: Ras2 farnesylation is critical for PKA activation.
source: It has been shown that Ras2 farnesylation is critical for PKA activation, suggesting that the signal we see for Erg20 is also the result of a perturbed Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway (Bhattacharya et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bhattacharya et al., 1995.

claim: Perturbations of inhibiting components of the Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway (Ira1/2, Bcy1, Mck1) decrease abundance of Tdh1 while increasing abundance of Tdh2 and Tdh3.
source: Conversely, perturbations of inhibiting components of this pathway (Ira1/2, Bcy1, Mck1) decrease abundance of Tdh1 while increasing abundance of Tdh2 and Tdh3 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LC-MS proteomics confirmed the effects of IRA2 and RAS2 mutations on Tdh1 and Tdh2 abundance.
source: We used LC-MS proteomics to confirm these findings in strains carrying engineered loss-of-function mutations in an inhibitor (IRA2) and an activator (RAS2) of the pathway (Figure 6D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent validation using LC-MS proteomics data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A functional connection between the Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway and Tdh1/Tdh2 is supported by the negative genetic interactions between TDH1/TDH2 and RAS2 reported in large-scale studies.
source: A functional connection between the Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway and Tdh1/Tdh2 is further supported by the negative genetic interactions between TDH1/TDH2 and RAS2 reported in large-scale studies (Costanzo et al., 2016; Costanzo et al., 2010; Oughtred et al., 2021; Srivas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costanzo et al., 2016; Costanzo et al., 2010; Oughtred et al., 2021; and Srivas et al., 2016.

claim: The gRNA predicted to introduce the RAS2 Q272* loss-of-function mutation increased abundance of Tdh1 and decreased abundance of Tdh2.
source: Ras2 Q272* increased abundance of Tdh1 and decreased abundance of Tdh2, while Ras2 S46L had the opposite effects (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The gRNA predicted to introduce the RAS2 S46L missense mutation decreased abundance of Tdh1 and increased abundance of Tdh2.
source: Ras2 Q272* increased abundance of Tdh1 and decreased abundance of Tdh2, while Ras2 S46L had the opposite effects (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The effect of the Ras2 S46L mutation on Tdh1 and Tdh2 was similar to that of a loss-of-function mutation of Ira2, a direct antagonist of Ras2.
source: The effect of the Ras2 S46L mutation on Tdh1 and Tdh2 was similar to that of a loss-of-function mutation of Ira2, a direct antagonist of Ras2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The observation that the S46L mutation activates Ras2 is consistent with the results of saturation mutagenesis of the highly conserved human K-Ras gene, which showed increased activity upon mutation of the homologous serine residue (S39 in human K-Ras) to leucine or valine.
source: Our observation that the S46L mutation activates Ras2 is consistent with the results of saturation mutagenesis of the highly conserved human K-Ras gene, which showed increased activity upon mutation of the homologous serine residue (S39 in human K-Ras) to leucine or valine (Bandaru et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study and is consistent with findings from Bandaru et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations of the serine residue homologous to yeast Ras2 S46 have been found in cervical cancers.
source: Mutations of this specific serine residue have been found in cervical cancers (COSMIC database, Tate et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the COSMIC database and Tate et al., 2018.

claim: When multiple gRNAs that introduce different mutations into the same gene had a significant effect on a protein's expression, their direction of effect was concordant in 98% of the cases.
source: When multiple gRNAs that introduce different mutations into the same gene had a significant effect on a protein's expression, their direction of effect was concordant in 98% of the cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the protein abundance screen.

claim: The correspondence between mRNA abundance and protein abundance is less strong than is usually implicitly assumed.
source: For practical reasons, mRNA abundance is often studied as a proxy for protein abundance, but the correspondence between the two is less strong than is usually implicitly assumed (Buccitelli and Selbach, 2020; Liu et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buccitelli and Selbach, 2020 and Liu et al., 2016a.
